title: March in Place: The Easiest Exercise for Beginners
intro: Marching in place is walking without going anywhere, great when it's raining, hot or you can't get out of the house. It's an easy way to add daily movement even if you only have a small space.
muscles: Thighs, glutes, calves and tummy muscles for stability. Good for heart stamina and adding to your daily step count.
steps: Stand tall, shoulders relaxed and look ahead.
Lift your right knee slightly, then put it down.
Lift your left knee, and keep alternating.
Swing your arms opposite to your legs, like normal walking.
Breathe normally and keep a comfortable pace.
mistakes: Hunching forward. Keep your chest open and head up.
Stomping your feet hard on the floor. Land softly so your joints feel better and your neighbours aren't disturbed.
Arms stiff by your sides. Swinging your arms helps raise your heart rate.
easier: Lift your feet only a little, hold the back of a chair, or sit on a chair and lift your knees alternately.
harder: Lift your knees to hip height, speed up the pace, or alternate 30 seconds fast and 30 seconds slow.
dose: Beginner: start with 10 minutes at a time. You can break it into 3 sessions x 10 minutes a day, for example while watching TV. Do it almost every day.
safety: Stop if you feel chest pain, unusual breathlessness or dizziness. If you have heart problems, uncontrolled high blood pressure or joint pain, ask your doctor first.

faq.q: Does marching in place really count as exercise?
faq.a: Yes. Every movement adds to the energy you use. For busy people, 10 minutes a few times a day helps a lot.

faq.q: Can I do it after eating?
faq.a: Yes, a slow 10-minute march after eating is okay. If you just ate a lot, start at a relaxed pace first.

faq.q: How many steps should I aim for?
faq.a: No need to chase a big number straight away. Look at your current average steps, then add 1,000-2,000 steps a day gradually.
